title: DXF export of Graded Nest broken after version 2025.0.252
content:
Using the latest version of Clo, 2025.0.252, the DXF output of graded nest patterns is missing data. You can clearly see this by looking at the file sizes, but also when trying to open the files in any other program.  
  
It appears that only the cutting lines (seam allowance) for a single size are output.![cbdaa89cc30d4c5ca1083e1f025ce5b0](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202507/1ce6e4dacdb841a1903da4d17bf6b047/images/cbdaa89cc30d4c5ca1083e1f025ce5b0Screenshot%202025-07-03%20155224.png)  
  
Older version:  
  
![9c845a5d334247068c5dc0ac610eec06](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202507/1ce6e4dacdb841a1903da4d17bf6b047/images/9c845a5d334247068c5dc0ac610eec06ResultingDXF_2025.0.252.png)  
Latest version:  
  
![515c8ef036bf4a0a8e8dc53aa2643735](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202507/1ce6e4dacdb841a1903da4d17bf6b047/images/515c8ef036bf4a0a8e8dc53aa2643735ResultingDXF_2025.0.408.png)

Notice the missing data. I can provide DXF's for comparison. Notice the difference in file size.  
  
![3f92c0290ab84d6f9bf719d6ebed4d4c](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202507/1ce6e4dacdb841a1903da4d17bf6b047/images/3f92c0290ab84d6f9bf719d6ebed4d4cScreenshot%202025-07-29%20084805.png)  
This affects ALL graded nest exports, and can be viewed in any program.  
The only work around I have is using older versions of Clo3d :(

### Community Post Comments:
Comment 1: Hello! I have just tested the latest version of Clo3D, and the same error appears in the Exporter. When exporting a graded pattern, only the cutting line for the selected size is exported! I had very much hoped this would have been fixed by now, as I am left using a very early version of the software, where the DXF export works correctly.
Reply 1: I have already supplied all the examples, explanations and output files necessary to test this. Indeed anyone with Clo3d can try this, exporting a DXF and opening in ANY OTHER SOFTWARE!
Reply 2: Hi Peter. If the issue continues you will need to start a ticket. We did find your old ticket number which is 113676. So you can reference that when you send it in.We do recommend being as clear as possible when sending it in. Sharing your EXACT workflow and what programs you use. (if Blender is NOT part of your workflow we recommend NOT mentioning it). Make sure to share screenshots of your exact Export and Import settings. Or even a screen recording showing the entire process step by step for the team to view and see what may be happening.If the files are too large then a WeTransfer link is a good option. Thank you 🙂

Comment 2: Hi Peter. There was an update this morning to 2025.0.416. Have you updated and tested on this version?
Reply 1: Hello, I can answer that question. I tried it and there is still no seam allowance on the other size of the grading. Kind of problematic to work with :/
Reply 2: Hi lucas. We are sorry to hear that. Are you using the latest 2026 release?If you are and are still having issues please send us the file directly through our tech support to look at.Please include the CLO file, and screen shots of your CLO export settings, screenshot of your Import settings and what program you are importing to. https://connect.clo-set.com/community/post/1ce6e4dacdb841a1903da4d17bf6b047
content_description: This page highlights a critical issue with the latest Clo 2025.0.252 update where graded nest DXF exports are missing data, affecting all graded nest outputs and requiring users to revert to older versions as a workaround.

title: How Lane Odom Took a CLO-Designed Bag All the Way to the Met
content:
## _From digital prototyping to the halls of the Met—_

##  _Designer_[ _Lane Odom_](https://www.instagram.com/lernonvane_/) _’s journey blends cultural storytelling, athletic discipline, and a sharp technical edge. In this spotlight, he shares how a simple favor for a friend became part of the Superfine: Tailoring Black Style exhibition, and how CLO helped bring that vision to life._  


* * *

**Can you introduce yourself and share a bit about your background?**

Absolutely. My name is Lane Odom, and I’m a designer and product developer currently working under the Coach brand, while building my own design studio called Vane Studios. Originally from the suburbs of Philadelphia, I’m a former collegiate athlete turned designer who was drawn to fashion through the opportunity to tell cultural stories and imagine character archetypes. Interestingly, it was a blend of my undergrad studies mixing anthropological problem solving with economics/business and it gave me a new hands on practice after I stopped playing Lacrosse. After completing the AAS program at Parsons, I’ve had the chance to work across a wide range of roles, spanning sportswear, menswear, tailoring, and womenswear.

![769f712f13ac4a5b8b5cc3a79909df4f](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202507/8e696642096242b2b68437ecd1e02ce9/images/769f712f13ac4a5b8b5cc3a79909df4fIMG_2548.JPG)

**This bag was featured in the “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style” exhibition at the Met. Could you tell us how this opportunity came about, and what it meant to be part of it?**

This opportunity was really unexpected and came about long after I initially worked on the project. I was helping my friend Jacques Agbobly round out their collection for February 2024 NYFW—doing pattern work on some cut-and-sew dresses that were later whole-garment knit, and creating an accessory for their trench coat, which is the bag featured in the Superfine lookbook. Honestly, it started out as a simple favor for a friend. 

So to see it end up in an exhibition like this means the world to me. Superfine speaks directly to the space I design from—the cultural history, pride, and nuance of Black style. What I find most powerful is that, when you look at the broader history of tailoring and fashion, the Black American aesthetic is still relatively young. Being able to contribute in any way to building that tradition is deeply meaningful. As a designer, I couldn’t ask for a better moment.

  
**How did you translate the artistic vision or cultural theme of the exhibition into your bag design using CLO?**

The design was really rooted in the Agbobly brand, especially the story of moving from Togo to the U.S., but we also pulled in some details that nod to the eccentricity of dandyism. One example is the pleated side patch pockets, which add a sense of character and flair. We also focused on a clean, classic duffle shape, which we adapted using a custom printed fabric. In doing so, we took something functional,almost mundane,and reimagined it with a new purpose and presence. The result is bold, and maybe even adds a layer of empowerment from the accessory to the wearer.

  
![f7f84fb8a4644d6eb4a19eafe5c56ab1](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202507/8e696642096242b2b68437ecd1e02ce9/images/f7f84fb8a4644d6eb4a19eafe5c56ab1AgboblyBag3-8.jpg)

**The print and silhouette of the bag are striking. While the print was created by @harlanhue, how did you approach incorporating it into your CLO design in terms of materials, scale, and visual composition?**

For this bag, proportion was everything, both in the design itself and in how we used the print. The bag has a good amount of seaming, so we wanted to make sure the print had enough room to breathe across each panel, without getting overly chopped up. CLO made that super manageable, we were able to drop the print onto the 3D asset and tweak the scale until it felt just right, even in those early development stages.

**Were there any technical or timeline challenges during this process?**

That said, we did run into some time constraints. Originally, we had a more complex strap system planned, but we had to pivot to a simpler version to meet the deadline. Hopefully for version two, we’ll get a chance to bring that first idea back to life.

**Can you walk us through your creative workflow for this project in CLO?**

I wish I had a more artistic story here—but honestly, this was a pretty technical process. Jacques shared the overall vision and some reference images for the kind of shape he wanted, so I started by focusing on construction—just building the right silhouette. A lot of it came down to understanding different bag structures and figuring out how to bring that to life in CLO.

Once I had the base shell completed, I started looking for elements from the broader collection that could tie into the bag. The pleats and bartacks, for example, were featured in some of the heavy canvas pieces, and I think I was able to successfully translate those details into a new fabrication.

  
![68d1d6e31c904850b196b8d620c993c6](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202507/8e696642096242b2b68437ecd1e02ce9/images/68d1d6e31c904850b196b8d620c993c6Screen%20Shot%202025-07-09%20at%2007.10.16.png)![8a36c8d26c3941dfa6a8e0682c4e0115](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202507/8e696642096242b2b68437ecd1e02ce9/images/8a36c8d26c3941dfa6a8e0682c4e0115Screen%20Shot%202025-07-09%20at%2007.03.48.png)

### **Was this your first time designing an accessory in CLO? If not, how does this project compare to your past works?**

I’ve designed a bag in CLO before and played around with shoe design in Blender, but this was the first accessory I’ve taken all the way from 3D to physical production. More recently, I also drafted a sun hat in CLO. This project definitely pushed me a bit further—mainly because it was the first time I actually built custom hardware in CLO3D. I always knew how, but I hadn’t worked on a project that really needed it until this one.

**Did you experiment with any unconventional techniques in CLO while designing this piece?**

The construction itself was pretty straightforward, but I definitely leaned on a few helpful tricks in CLO. Turning off gravity was a big one—it made the whole process a lot smoother. I also separated the bottom of the bag from the sides in the software, even though it’s actually one pattern piece in real life. Freezing that bottom piece really helped stabilize everything while I worked on the rest of the design.

### **What do you think is the future potential of CLO as a tool for artistic or exhibition-focused design?**

The potential of CLO is honestly huge. What makes it so powerful is how it supports both physical and digital asset creation at the same time. This was my first time ever making a duffle bag, and the fact that I could get such a clean result in just one sample round says a lot about how it can streamline the development process.

From a creative standpoint, being able to design without the limits of real-world physics is amazing. We had originally planned to add these long, flowing straps to the bag, there just wasn’t time to develop them physically. But in CLO, we could still show them, and even make them interactive if we wanted.

To me, CLO is just the start of where fashion and tech are headed. I think we’ll keep seeing more crossover, from digital software all the way to smart textiles and beyond.

  
![45b00d275abc4f0cb4956910b02f8663](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202507/8e696642096242b2b68437ecd1e02ce9/images/45b00d275abc4f0cb4956910b02f8663IMG_1158.jpeg)

### **Many CLO users are exploring accessories and more artistic applications. What advice would you give to someone using CLO to create beyond traditional garments?**

My biggest piece of advice? Don’t forget the real world. Use physical references as you design. Early on, when I first started using CLO, I often skipped that step and worked entirely digitally. But I found myself having to backtrack when it came time to translate those ideas into something physical.

Even if your goal is to stay purely digital, making sure your work reflects real-world scale and proportion goes a long way. It adds a layer of believability and accuracy that builds trust, especially as digital/phygital fashion continues to gain adoption within the industry.   


* * *

 _Full look by_[ _@agbobly_](https://www.instagram.com/agbobly/) _| bag print by_[ _@harlanhue_](https://www.instagram.com/harlanhue/)

 _Photography_[ _@tylersphotos_](https://www.instagram.com/tylersphotos/)  
 _Styling_[ _@mr_carlos_nazario_](https://www.instagram.com/mr_carlos_nazario/)  
 _Hair_[ _@dre_on_hair_](https://www.instagram.com/dre_on_hair/)

content_description: Showcasing designer Lane Odom’s creative journey and technical process using CLO to bring culturally rich, exhibition-featured accessories from digital prototype to physical reality.
